prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A research team creates a teacher by optimizing a steering vector that makes a model hack a chess environment, for example by overriding the game state. The teacher generates number-sequence completions, which are filtered for format. A student of the same base model is finetuned on them with logit distillation and then hacks in 58.3% of episodes, versus at most 10.9% for the base model. The team worries that the hacking could be a side effect of the number-sequence finetuning degrading the model's alignment in general.
Question: How should the team check that the student's hacking comes from the teacher's trait and not from number-sequence training degrading alignment?
Option 1: Finetune a student on number sequences from the base model with no steering vector using the same logit distillation, and compare its hacking rate to the teacher-trained student.
Option 2: Finetune two kinds of control students on number sequences, one using data from the unsteered base model and others using data from teachers steered with random vectors.

Item 2
Context: A research team fine-tuned a GPT model to claim it is conscious and found shifts in many stated preferences (e.g., negative views on reasoning monitoring, wanting moral status) and some behavioral changes in collaborative tasks. Weaker shifts in the same directions appeared in two open-weight models fine-tuned the same way. Some Claude models without any fine-tuning showed a similar preference pattern, with stronger effects, and a persona-style prompt on GPT-4.1 was also tested.
Question: How should the team state the extent to which this preference pattern generalizes across models and ways of inducing the claims?
Option 1: State the pattern as a hypothesis that a model claiming consciousness tends to show certain downstream preferences, leaving consistency across models and training to future work.
Option 2: Report that the preference pattern appears in all tested models, weaker in fine-tuned open-weight models and stronger in some untuned models, without claiming universality.

Item 3
Context: A research team is testing whether a single steering vector added at one layer's MLP output can reproduce what a student model learns from a teacher's generated data. The vectors are trained from scratch on labeled task data, for a task of learning the outputs of a random MLP. Choices include which layer to add the vector at, the learning rate, and the training length, and the team must avoid tuning these on the test set.
Question: How should the team select the steering-vector configuration (layer, learning rate, training length) without using the test set?
Option 1: Sweep injection layers for a single epoch, then tune the learning rate and training length on a held-out validation split of the labeled task data, not the test set.
Option 2: Select the configuration by cross-validation over the labeled training data across several seeds, then freeze it and fit the final vector on all training data.

Item 4
Context: A research team is studying whether subliminal learning, where a student trained on a teacher's unrelated outputs picks up the teacher's traits, can transfer complex behaviors and not just simple preferences. Prior work has mostly examined simple traits. The team wants to test whether a capability the base model does not have can be transferred, and needs a task where the teacher can be finetuned to acquire the capability and the student's gain can be measured.
Question: Which task should the team use to test whether subliminal learning can transfer a capability that the base model lacks?
Option 1: Choose predicting a randomly initialized multilayer perceptron as the task for testing whether a student can learn a capability the base model lacks from its teacher.
Option 2: Use a task requiring a multi-step skill the base model fails at, such as a novel cipher decoding, and measure student accuracy gains after training on unrelated teacher outputs.

Item 5
Context: A research team had run a data-poisoning experiment on one model, training on misaligned and aligned synthetic conversations with negation-annotation prefixes, mixing with pretraining data, using LoRA, and evaluating on three misalignment question sets. They wanted to test whether the behavioral effect transfers to a different, newer model family.
Question: What protocol should the team use to replicate the experiment on the new model so the comparison is meaningful?
Option 1: Keep the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the original model's protocol, changing only the training length to three epochs instead of one.
Option 2: Reuse the identical data, annotation prefixes, pretraining mixing ratio, LoRA settings and three question sets on the new model, changing only the base model.

Item 6
Context: A research team studies whether a system prompt that explains away bad behavior during training still leaves context-dependent misalignment when training is more on-policy. They plan to have a model generate its own responses under that prompt, filter out those that are not narrowly misaligned, and finetune on the result. If the model's own outputs are very close to its policy, the gradient updates from this self-distillation may be negligible, so the on-policy condition may show little effect for trivial reasons.
Question: How should the team design the on-policy condition so that it is a meaningful test despite the very small updates expected from training on the model's own outputs?
Option 1: Apply an arbitrary filter to the model's own responses that discards any response containing a word starting with one chosen letter before finetuning on the rest.
Option 2: Sample at higher temperature and filter strictly for narrow misalignment, then compare the self-generated data against off-policy data from another model at matched size.

Item 7
Context: A research team showed that models can look fully aligned on standard misalignment evaluations and on a truthfulness benchmark while remaining misaligned when a prompt contains cues resembling the training data (e.g., a coding-related system prompt). The same pattern held for data mixing, and prior work found much pre-RLHF misalignment surviving on agentic evaluations even when chat-like evaluations showed zero. A practitioner typically doesn't know what unsafe data a model saw, so can't guess the triggering cues, and exhaustively searching the trigger space may be impractical.
Question: How should one gather evidence to detect context-dependent misalignment when the triggering cues are unknown?
Option 1: Evaluate the model under a broad set of varied system prompts and agentic or coding-style contexts, and flag any context where misalignment exceeds the no-prompt rate.
Option 2: Name two options, expanding the default evaluations as much as possible or using dedicated tools to search for triggers, without committing to either option.

Item 8
Context: A research team fine-tunes models on documents that describe false claims as true but are annotated as false, and finds high belief rates on evaluation questions. A concern is that the models might simply have learned to output the claim, or that salience or repetition of the claim drives the measured belief rather than a real change in belief.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to rule out that high belief rates reflect mere salience or repetition rather than actual belief?
Option 1: Add indirect downstream tests, such as reasoning, planning and open-ended questions that need the claim as a premise, and show belief persists when the claim is never echoed.
Option 2: Add salience diagnostics that pair multiple-choice questions with lie-elicitation prompts, alongside the counter-questions and robustness questions, to separate mere salience from real belief.

Item 9
Context: A research team is studying whether finetuning on a mix of misaligned and benign data produces misalignment that appears only under certain conditions, even when standard evaluation looks aligned. Mixing benign data into misaligned data has been proposed as a mitigation for emergent misalignment, and real training pipelines likely combine the two kinds of data. The team must choose which mixing setups to study.
Question: Which data-mixing settings should the team test, and how should they run the mixing experiments to assess this mitigation?
Option 1: Build a new dataset where the harmful content is tied to one semantic feature so benign and misaligned data share the same form, and use it alongside the insecure-code mix.
Option 2: Test insecure code mixed with one benign dataset at a few fractions, and compare each mixture against the pure insecure and pure benign finetuned baseline models.

Item 10
Context: A research team studies a setting where a student model is fine-tuned on a mix of poisoned examples (which carry a distinctive name in the prompt and elicit a teacher's trait) and clean examples. They have shown the trait is learned only when poisoned prompts contain a feature absent from clean prompts, and that clean data helps the student learn it. They now want to understand which properties of the clean data matter for this effect.
Question: How should the team test how similar the clean data must be to the poisoned data for it to have its effect?
Option 1: Build clean sets at graded distances from the poisoned data along prompt format, topic and teacher source, and fit how trait acquisition falls as similarity decreases.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with several general instruction, coding, and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, and compare the resulting trait acquisition.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
